I'm confused, why do these all need to be parameterized?  The timers should basically never run in a unit test (ie all timeouts should be infinity, and unit test should call timeout functions directly).  Even so, I'm not sure why making every one of these timeouts different helps unit tests.
See next patch, i am not only looking for unit tests. So there are different requirements.

Which patch is "next patch"?  https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/entity-manager/+/85557

doesn't appear to use these.

1. This needs some kind of object to hold them.  We're at the "too many constructor arguments" phase, certainly if all the types are the same.
2. If we're needing all these timeouts in unit tests, I worry that we're not writing the "unit" part of the unit tests, and this class is doing too much.  We should be able to trigger each of these manually without needing to rely on the timeout itself, right?

> This needs some kind of object to hold them. We're at the "too many constructor arguments" phase, certainly if all the types are the same.

Sure, i can try to come up with a class to hold these parameters.

> We should be able to trigger each of these manually without needing to rely on the timeout itself, right?

How? It's various calls buried in EM code. We would need to restructure all of that to callbacks or something for the test to be able to intervene.

That sounds like it would complicate the EM code further.

> > This needs some kind of object to hold them. We're at the "too many constructor arguments" phase, certainly if all the types are the same.
> 
> Sure, i can try to come up with a class to hold these parameters.
> 
> > We should be able to trigger each of these manually without needing to rely on the timeout itself, right?
> 
> How? It's various calls buried in EM code. We would need to restructure all of that to callbacks or something for the test to be able to intervene.

Yes, exactly this.

> 
> That sounds like it would complicate the EM code further.

I don't agree that abstracting code to make smaller functions complicates things further.  Maybe it's "more code", but it should be simpler (and now unit tested) code.
